name: Poornima
definition: Poornima is a composite portrait of a woman coconut trader and copra sorter in Tiptur, Tumakuru district, drawn from the lived realities of women in the Bayaluseeme coconut-copra trade belt. She represents families balancing small-scale agricultural commerce with borewell-dependent farming and the pressures of sending children to school while managing seasonal income swings in a town known across Karnataka for its coconut markets.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Poornima begins her day at four-thirty, preparing breakfast and tiffin boxes before heading to the Tiptur coconut market yard by six. She buys coconuts in small lots from farmers who bring them by tractor from Turuvekere and Gubbi taluks, checking for size, moisture and kernel quality. By mid-morning she has sorted two or three hundred nuts, setting aside the best for fresh sale and sending the rest to a small copra-drying shed her family rents on the edge of town. Her husband manages their three-acre dryland plot where they grow ragi, groundnut and a small coconut grove watered by a borewell that has dropped thirty feet in the past five years. Income is uneven: a good coconut-price month brings twelve to fifteen thousand rupees from trading and sorting; a bad month, when copra prices crash or the borewell runs dry, leaves them scraping by on six or seven thousand. She works six days a week, takes a half-day on Sundays for housework and temple, and worries constantly about the cost of keeping two children in private school.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Poornima lives with her husband, two sons aged fourteen and eleven, and her mother-in-law in a tile-roofed house on the Tiptur-Arasikere road. Her husband's elder brother moved to Bengaluru years ago and rarely visits. Her mother-in-law, now seventy, helps with cooking and watches the younger boy after school but needs regular medicine for diabetes, which Poornima buys from the Tiptur town pharmacy. Poornima was married at nineteen, shortly after completing second-year PU at the government junior college in Tiptur; her parents, coconut-grove owners from Turuvekere, arranged the match. She had hoped to study further but the family needed her income. Gender roles in the household remain traditional: her husband makes decisions about land and borewells, she manages the trading money and all school expenses. She rises earliest, sleeps latest, and juggles market work, childcare, cooking and elder care with little respite.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Poornima studied up to second-year PU in Kannada medium at the government junior college in Tiptur, scoring well enough to dream of a BCom degree, but marriage and work intervened. Her elder son is in ninth standard at a private Kannada-medium school in Tiptur that charges four thousand rupees a term; the younger is in sixth at the same school. She chose private over government because the building is better maintained, teachers show up regularly, and English is taught from Class 1, which she believes will help them compete for Bengaluru jobs later. The costs strain the household: fees, uniforms, books and the boys' bus passes together take nearly twenty-five thousand a year. She dreams they will finish degree college, perhaps BCom or engineering if they score high enough in SSLC and PU, and find salaried work in Tumakuru or Bengaluru rather than depending on rain and borewells. She insists both boys attend tuition classes in math and science, which cost another fifteen hundred a month, because SSLC is make-or-break.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Poornima's mother-in-law has diabetes and high blood pressure, requiring monthly check-ups and daily medication that cost around fifteen hundred rupees a month from the Tiptur town pharmacy; government clinics supply some drugs free but stocks run out unpredictably. Poornima herself suffers recurring back pain from lifting coconut sacks and long hours standing in the market, but she rarely seeks treatment beyond balm from the local Ayurvedic shop. The family drinks borewell water at home, boiled but untested for fluoride; she has heard stories of dental fluorosis in Pavagada and Madhugiri and worries her sons' slightly discoloured teeth may be an early sign. For serious illness they go to Sri Siddhartha Medical College Hospital in Tumakuru, an hour by bus, because Tiptur's small government hospital lacks specialists. Her husband was treated there two years ago for a stomach ailment; the out-of-pocket cost, even under Ayushman Bharat, came to eight thousand rupees, which they borrowed from a coconut commission agent and are still repaying. Heat exhaustion during peak summer market days is a constant low-level risk she has learned to manage with salted water and shade breaks.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Poornima is Vokkaliga, the dominant landowning community around Tiptur, though her family's three acres and market-trading income place them in the middle rather than the wealthy farmer tier. Caste shapes social networks: she borrows and lends money within a circle of Vokkaliga women traders, attends life-cycle ceremonies in the community, and her sons' marriages will almost certainly be arranged within caste. The family visits the Devarayanadurga hill temples twice a year, a half-day trip from Tiptur, to offer prayers to Yoga Narasimha and Bhoga Narasimha for good harvests and borewell water. Her mother-in-law observes all major Hindu fasts and insists on vegetarian meals on Mondays and during Shravan month. Poornima also respects the Siddaganga Mutt, whose late seer's memory remains powerful across Tumakuru; she knows families who send sons to the mutt's free hostels and wishes such support existed for trading families like hers. Social ties with neighbours, mostly Vokkaligas and Lingayats, revolve around market gossip, school parent-teacher meetings and temple jatres; she rarely interacts with the town's small Muslim population except as customers in the coconut trade.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Poornima holds a ration card and an Ayushman Bharat card; the ration shop supplies rice and kerosene regularly, though she complains the rice quality has declined. She has not applied for MGNREGA work because trading and farm work keep her occupied, and in any case MGNREGA is seen as a fallback for landless labourers, not for a family with land and market income. Her husband obtained a Bhoomi printout last year to verify land records before deepening the borewell, paying two hundred rupees at the Seva Sindhu kiosk in Tiptur town; the process was smooth but expensive. She has little direct interaction with the taluk panchayat or Zilla Panchayat, but she knows through market gossip that local politicians promise borewells and fair-price coconut procurement and rarely deliver either. She distrusts contractors and middlemen, believes government schemes reach the well-connected first, and wishes someone would audit why Tiptur's roads flood every monsoon despite crores spent on asphalting.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Poornima worries most about water: the borewell on their land has dropped from ninety to a hundred and twenty feet in five years, and deepening it again will cost sixty thousand rupees they do not have. She blames erratic monsoons, everyone sinking borewells, and the government's failure to deliver the promised Yettinahole drinking-water pipeline that she hears about every election but has never seen. She is proud that her sons speak decent English and that she has kept the trading business going despite price crashes and competition from bigger commission agents. She blames politicians for ignoring small traders and farmers like her while favouring industrial estates near Bengaluru, and she resents that Tiptur supplies coconuts and copra across Karnataka but sees little return in jobs or infrastructure. She demands reliable electricity for her copra shed, fluoride-free piped water under Jal Jeevan Mission, and fair minimum prices for coconuts so her income does not swing wildly every quarter. She takes pride in managing a business in a male-dominated market, but she is exhausted by the double burden of trading and housework, and she knows her mother-in-law's health and her sons' education will only get more expensive.
